t: Hawaiian religion is polytheistic and animistic: Kāne, Kū, Lono and Kanaloa are especially prominent among many gods, and every Native Hawaiian family was considered to have one or more guardian spirits, the ʻaumākua.

The kapu system, a set of taboos separating the spiritually pure from the potentially unclean, ruled daily life until 1819, when Kamehameha II, persuaded by two of his father's wives and the kahuna nui Hewahewa, overthrew it.

Missionaries arrived from 1820 and most aliʻi converted, but family ʻaumākua, veneration of bones and sacred places survived, and a Hawaiian Renaissance in the 1970s brought a resurgence of the religion.
dyk: In the Kumulipo, the man Kiʻi succeeds in seducing and reproducing with the woman Laʻilaʻi before the god Kāne has the chance, so the divine lineage becomes younger than, and subservient to, the lineage of humankind.
ev: Settlers from the Marquesas and greater Polynesia have reached the Hawaiian Islands by this date, bringing their religious beliefs
By tradition Pāʻao, a priest or chief from Tahiti, arrives in Hawaiʻi and brings the kapu system
After the death of Kamehameha the Great, Kaʻahumanu and Keōpūolani confer with the kahuna nui Hewahewa and persuade Liholiho, Kamehameha II, to overthrow the kapu system
Protestant Christian missionaries begin to arrive from the United States and gain great influence in the Kingdom of Hawaii
The American author Max Freedom Long originates the philosophy and practice he calls Huna
Members of Protect Kahoʻolawe ʻOhana file suit over the Navy's use of Kahoʻolawe for target practice, citing cultural and religious sites
The unearthing of 1,000 graves during construction of a hotel on Maui leads to its redesign and relocation inland
Protests begin on the Island of Hawaii over the choice of Mauna Kea for the Thirty Meter Telescope

f.origin: The Hawaiian Islands, brought by Tahitians and other Pacific Islanders who landed there between 500 and 1300 CE; there is significant evidence of settlement no later than 800 CE, with immigration continuing to about 1300 CE, from the Marquesas and greater Polynesia.
f.founder: none: it arose among Polynesian settlers and evolved over time and from place to place; tradition says the kapu system arrived with Pāʻao, a priest or chief from Tahiti, around 1200 CE.
f.scriptures: none written: the Kumulipo, an epic chant linking the aliʻi, or Hawaiian royalty, to the gods, and the prayers, chants and traditions of the kahuna and families, handed down orally.
f.followers: No figure is given: traditional practices survive through family ʻaumākua, the veneration of iwi (bones) and the care of sacred places; some Hawaiians practise Christianised versions of old traditions, others the old faith as a co-religion.
